props.title: Reversal of Fortune
props.initialSlug: Rich wife in coma: husband's bizarre trial unfolds

sections.content: Reversal of Fortune (1990) revolutionized the true-crime legal drama by breaking the fourth wall and letting accused attempted murderer Claus von Bülow (Jeremy Irons) directly address viewers. Director Barbet Schroeder crafted a wickedly ambiguous portrait that questions truth itself, using von Bülow's appeal case as a lens to examine class privilege, justice, and moral relativity. The film's innovative structure - narrated by Glenn Close as the comatose Sunny von Bülow - creates an unsettling disconnect between what we're told and what we see. This technique influenced later true-crime narratives like The Thin Blue Line (1988) and JFK (1991).

sections.content: The film marked a turning point in legal dramas, moving away from straightforward courtroom theatrics toward morally ambiguous territory. While To Kill a Mockingbird (1962) and 12 Angry Men (1957) presented clear moral positions, Reversal of Fortune revels in uncertainty. This influenced sophisticated legal thrillers like Michael Clayton (2007) and Dark Waters (2019), which explore the grey areas between truth and justice.

Jeremy Irons' Oscar-winning performance as von Bülow set a new standard for portraying real-life figures. His elegant, reptilian charm makes the character simultaneously fascinating and repulsive - a technique later employed in films like The Social Network (2010) and Vice (2018). The film's exploration of wealth and privilege in the justice system predates similar themes in The People vs. O.J. Simpson (2016) and Molly's Game (2017). sections.content: Reversal of Fortune pioneered techniques now common in true-crime documentaries and dramatizations. Its unreliable narration and multiple perspectives influenced works like I, Tonya (2017) and American Animals (2018). The film's cold, analytical approach to upper-class crime created a template followed by All Good Things (2010) and Bernie (2011).
